🕶️ Hello, Monday. Sorry: It's the last day of August! Smart Brevity™ count: 1,380 words ... 5 mins. Thanks to Erica Pandey for orchestrating. Edited by Ben Berkowitz and Bill Kole.

🇳🇵 Situational awareness: The death toll in the historic Nepal and China floods topped 900, with nearly 5,000 still missing. Read the latest.
 
 
1 big thing: AI's reputation fix
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

AI has an image problem — and one way to fix it is for top companies to dive headlong into health care, Axios' Adriel Bettelheim writes in Axios Future of Health Care.

  • Why it matters: Saving the world with AI-designed cures is better than being blamed for ruining the environment or driving up Americans' utility bills.

🩺 The Wall Street Journal reported this month that Anthropic is trying to shore up investor confidence ahead of its massive initial public offering with talk of pushing harder into health care and biotech.

  • Anthropic isn't alone: Nvidia and Eli Lilly are building a $1 billion drug-discovery lab in San Francisco that will team life-sciences researchers with AI model builders and engineers.
  • Isomorphic Labs, the AI drug-discovery spinoff from Google, recently raised $2.1 billion to hire more AI and clinical talent and has ongoing research collaborations with Novartis, Lilly and Johnson & Johnson.

💡 Reality check: AI is dramatically speeding up drug development and helping clinicians analyze medical scans and diagnose conditions. But there are concerns that AI-enabled research tools could be used for nefarious purposes, including making a biological weapon.

  • And breakthroughs may still be years away.

Read on ... Sign up for Axios Future of Health Care, our daily briefing on the policy moves, business trends and innovations reshaping health care.
 
 
2. 💥 Socialist war over AOC
 

Photo illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Photo: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call via Getty Images
 

A potential 2028 presidential run by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) has exposed long-simmering divisions within the Democratic Socialists of America.

  • Why it matters: The socialism movement's leaders are increasingly at odds over who should speak for them, what policies they stand for — and whether to support AOC, whom some dismiss as more establishment than insurgent, Axios' Alex Thompson and Holly Otterbein report.

AOC was the focus of internal fights this summer: The national DSA voted to keep more control of the group's 2028 endorsement process, which some local chapters saw as an attempt to stop a quick AOC endorsement.

  • "We're not in a book club anymore," said one strategist who works with the DSA. "You could be growing this organization by pointing to AOC, Bernie [Sanders], [Zohran] Mamdani — and instead they are going on cable news talking about abolishing the Senate, Fidel Castro and other weird stuff. It's a blown opportunity."

3. 🪖 U.S. strikes Iranian mine launchers
 
Ships are anchored in the Strait of Hormuz. Photo: Ali Saeedi/Getty Images

The U.S. military struck Iranian military targets to prevent the deployment of sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz, a U.S. official told Axios' Barak Ravid.

  • Why it matters: This is the first known U.S. strike in Iran since late July.

Iran retaliated with limited attacks on both the UAE and Jordan.

  • Oil surged 3% after the exchange of fire.

Threat level: President Trump posted an apparent AI video overnight that he said showed Iran's crucial Kharg Island oil terminal being "blown to smithereens."

  • Seizing or destroying Kharg, the heart of Iran's oil industry, has been one of his regular threats during the war.

The U.S. military last week finished clearing all mines from the strait's main shipping lane.

  • Trump said then that Iran was notified that any ship or boat placing new mines would be "immediately and systematically destroyed."

4. 🥳 Happy 50th to the first index fund
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios
 

The OG stock index fund, the Vanguard 500, turns 50 years old today.

  • Why it matters: Passive funds ate the world. Today, index funds make up 64% of all stock fund assets, and millions of investors use them, Axios markets correspondent Emily Peck writes.

Most of us are socking away money in these things automatically through 401(k) payroll deductions.

  • Stat du jour: If you'd put $10,000 in the Vanguard 500 back in 1976, it'd be worth over $2 million today.

5. 🗳️ El-Sayed courts Jewish Democrats
 
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee from Michigan, speaks to reporters in Lansing, Mich., on Saturday. Photo: Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Michigan Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed spent the weekend trying to make amends with the state's Jewish Democrats. But he showed there are limits to how far he's willing to go.

  • The big one: Hasan Piker.

Why it matters: El-Sayed's appearance before the state party's Jewish caucus was an important early test of whether he can pivot from a primary candidate who electrified the party's progressive wing to a general-election nominee who can win over moderate voters uneasy with his politics, Axios' Mike Zapler writes.

🔎 Catch up quick: El-Sayed apologized for his comments after a March attack on a suburban Detroit synagogue. It was attempted by a Lebanese-born man who lost relatives in an Israeli airstrike in Lebanon the week before.

  • El-Sayed initially condemned the attack. Then, the next day, he released a four-minute video in which he called it "an evil act of displaced rage" but also said that "hurt people hurt people."

What he said: El-Sayed on Saturday said he regretted those March comments.

  • "I made a mistake," he told the Jewish caucus. "I should have issued a statement, of course, condemning it. And it just should have been the full stop."
  • "We condemned that terrorist attack. … What I was trying to do is offer context for why it happened, but it wasn't the time for context. And you don't ever want to trample somebody's pain," El-Sayed told reporters afterward.

What he didn't say: El-Sayed keeps being asked to repudiate Piker, the incendiary left-wing streamer. He keeps refusing.

  • Asked repeatedly by reporters Saturday about Piker, El-Sayed wouldn't engage. "If you want to make this race about a streamer in California, I just think you're missing the boat," he said. He later said he was "not interested in a conversation about a social media person in California."

6. 💰 AI group plans data-center push in battlegrounds
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Build American AI — an advocacy group tied to pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future — is spending big on the data-center fight, with plans to pour millions of dollars into battleground states after Labor Day, according to an announcement shared first with Axios' Maria Curi.

  • Why it matters: The data-center backlash is becoming a defining issue of the midterms, and supporters of the developments are punching back.

Build American AI, a 501(c)(4) nonprofit, has about $50 million cash on hand. The group's campaign will begin in Kansas, Ohio and Wisconsin.

  • The money will go toward paid advertising, grassroots engagement, research, earned media and public education.

💡 The message: The U.S. should build the infrastructure needed to lead the world in AI while protecting families, communities and the environment.

  • The group said the campaign will expand as state legislatures develop bills for 2027 sessions.
  • The advocacy group is also launching a new super PAC — Building the Future (a 527) — to back state and federal candidates aligned with its agenda and oppose those who aren't.

Build American AI is pointing to Colorado, Georgia and Texas as models for how states should approach data-center development:

  • Colorado Gov. Jared Polis (D) has been bullish on data centers. Georgia offers data-center tax exemptions.
  • Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) has spoken harshly of data centers in recent weeks, including requiring companies to pay their own infrastructure costs and pausing new grid approvals pending an audit.

7. 🗺️ Lake America is live
 

Screenshots of Google Maps and Apple Maps taken yesterday morning.
 

President Trump's order to rename Lake Ontario to "Lake America" is splitting digital map providers:

  • Google Maps now says "Lake America." Apple Maps is sticking with Lake Ontario.
  • MapQuest said: "We're not changing the name of Lake Ontario. Name it whatever you want at your leisure."
Photo: Keito Newman/The Canadian Press via AP

Above: Ontario Premier Doug Ford (right) unveiled this sign Saturday in Grimsby, Ontario, Canada.

8. 🎥 1 film thing: Wile E. Coyote's back
 
Wile E. Coyote, voiced by Eric Bauza, in "Coyote vs. Acme." Photo: Ketchup Entertainment via AP

The abrupt termination of "Coyote vs. Acme" sent shockwaves through Hollywood.

  • Everyone in the movie business is accustomed to sudden, painful twists of fate. But the wholesale elimination of a finished film faster than you can say "Meep! Meep!" was something new.

But nearly three years later, the movie is, like its ever-undaunted protagonist, back from the dead.

  • After an outcry, Warner Bros. put "Coyote vs. Acme" up for sale. Ketchup Entertainment, an independent distributor that last year released the Looney Tunes movie "The Day the Earth Blew Up," picked it up for about $50 million. Now it's in theaters.

The movie opened with a respectable $15 million box-office haul, second only to the juggernaut that is "Spider-Man."
